title: Padmasambhava
hook: the tradition tells how Guru Rinpoche tamed the forces blocking the teaching in Tibet

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shantarakshita, the abbot who, when trouble came, named another teacher. Your line: the invitation.

In Tibetan paintings he sits in layered robes, a lotus hat topped with a feather, a staff resting in the crook of his arm, a vajra in his hand, his eyes wide open. Tibetans call him Guru Rinpoche, the precious teacher. The abbot from India named him. The king sent for him. And according to the story, on his way in, the land itself rose up to stop him.
screen: `A LOTUS HAT, A STAFF, WIDE EYES.` → `GURU RINPOCHE.` → `THE LAND RISES AGAINST HIM.`

segments.voice: His name is Sanskrit: Padmasambhava, born from a lotus. Tradition tells the story behind it: he appeared as a child sitting in a lotus on a lake in the land of Oddiyana. He's a tantric master, a yogi of power rather than an abbot of rules, which is exactly why the abbot named him. On his road into Tibet, the stories say, the spirits of the mountains, lakes and passes rose up to block him with storms, landslides and sickness. Here's the surprising turn. He didn't destroy them. He tamed them. One after another, the accounts say, he subdued these forces and bound them by oath to protect the teaching. The very powers that blocked the road became its guardians. Tibetan temples honor protectors who, in the story, began as its enemies. So tamed is the precise word. A tamed horse still has all its strength; it just stops throwing the rider. Some Tibetan teachers read this story two ways at once, without asking anyone to choose. Outwardly, it's how the teaching settled into a land that already had its own spirits. Inwardly, it's a map of the mind. Anger, fear and pride rise up against practice. In this reading they needn't be wiped out. They can be brought under oath, and their energy turned toward the path. The Nyingma, the old school of Tibetan Buddhism, looks to Padmasambhava as its founder.
screen: `BORN FROM A LOTUS.` · `THE SPIRITS BLOCK THE ROAD.` · `TAMED, NOT DESTROYED.` · `OUTWARD HISTORY, INWARD MAP.` · then, large: `THE OBSTACLES TAMED.`

segments.voice: Name one thing blocking your road right now, a worry, an irritation, a habit, and without fighting it, notice where it sits in the body. Ask it quietly what its strength could be for: worry might become care, anger might become courage for what's right. If it won't be tamed today, that's fine; let it be there, and keep breathing.
Padmasambhava. Born from a lotus. Guru Rinpoche, who, tradition says, tamed the forces blocking the teaching in Tibet and made them its guardians.
Your line: the obstacles tamed. Taming isn't killing; the strength stays. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists, especially in the Nyingma school, recite Padmasambhava's mantra, keep his image on their shrines, and hold feast days in his honor.

chat.says: Did Padmasambhava destroy the spirits that tried to block him?
options: No. The story says he tamed them and bound them by oath to protect the teaching.
Yes. He wiped out every one of them, so Tibet had no spirits left at all.
No. He ran from them and went home, and the abbot finished alone.
